title: Partition and Bend
focus: Selection without full sorting, the hardest monotonic stack, and the DP that thinks backwards.

cards.title: Quickselect
patterns: Partition, then recurse on one side
cards.trigger: Kth largest or smallest, and you are allowed to mutate the array.
cards.recall: Write it from memory. Then answer the two complexity questions: why is the average O(n), why is the worst case O(n^2), and what makes the difference?
useWhen: Kth largest or smallest element
Top k elements when you do not need them in order
Median of an unsorted array
Wiggle sort II, after finding the median
Any selection where a full sort is more than the question asks for
template: target = len(nums) - k          # index it would occupy when sorted ascending
elif p < target:  lo = p + 1     # recurse RIGHT only
else:             hi = p - 1     # recurse LEFT only
r = random.randint(lo, hi)          # random pivot defeats sorted input

problem.name: Kth Largest Element in an Array

keyInsights: Only one side is recursed into, so the work is n + n/2 + n/4 and that sums to 2n. That is the linear argument
Without a random pivot, an already-sorted array gives you every partition of size one and quadratic time
It mutates the input and gives no ordering among the top k. If either matters, use a heap
cards.trap: 'Guarantee O(n) worst case.' That is median-of-medians. Name it, say it is linear but with a bad constant, and that randomised quickselect is what you would actually ship.

cards.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
patterns: Width from the new left neighbour
cards.trigger: Maximal area or span bounded by a smaller element on each side.
cards.recall: Write it from memory. Then answer the line that carries everything: when you pop index `top`, what is the width of its rectangle, and why is `stack[-1]` the correct left bound after the pop?
useWhen: Largest rectangle in a histogram
Maximal rectangle in a binary matrix, row by row
Sum of subarray minimums, or maximums
Trapping rain water, the stack formulation
Any 'extend until a smaller element blocks you' question
template: heights.append(0)                    # sentinel flushes the stack at the end
stack, best = [], 0                  # stack holds indices, heights increasing
left = stack[-1] if stack else -1   # nearest smaller to the LEFT
width = i - left - 1               # i is nearest smaller to the RIGHT
# Maximal rectangle in a 0/1 matrix: build a running histogram per row,
# reset a column to 0 when the cell is 0, and call the above on each row.
keyInsights: After popping, `stack[-1]` is the nearest strictly smaller bar to the left, because everything between was already popped
The current index i is the nearest smaller bar to the right, which is exactly why the pop happens now
Maximal rectangle is this function called n times on a running histogram. Seeing that reduces a hard problem to a known one
cards.trap: 'Equal heights.' With `>` you pop later and still get the right maximum, because the taller-equal bar's own pop covers the full width. Be ready to argue that, it looks like a bug.

cards.title: Tree as an Undirected Graph
patterns: Track visited to avoid going back
cards.trigger: Distance or reachability in a tree measured from an arbitrary node, not from the root.
cards.recall: Write all-nodes-distance-k from memory. Then answer: why does the tree need converting to an undirected graph at all, and what is the one extra thing BFS needs that it did not need on the rooted tree?
useWhen: All nodes at distance k from a target
Amount of time for a whole binary tree to be infected
Closest leaf to a given node
Tree diameter via two BFS runs
Any tree question where the origin is not the root
template: for nxt in (n.left, n.right, parent[n]):   # THREE neighbours now
if nxt and nxt not in seen:

problem.name: All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree

keyInsights: A rooted tree only points downwards. Distance is symmetric, so you need the upward edge too
Once parents exist, every node has up to three neighbours and it is an ordinary undirected graph BFS
A visited set becomes mandatory. On a rooted traversal you never revisit; here you would bounce straight back to the parent
cards.trap: 'Do it without a parent map.' You can, with an annotated DFS that returns the distance to the target and handles the subtree split, and it is considerably harder to get right.

cards.title: Last-Move Interval DP
cards.trigger: Actions interfere with each other, and choosing what happens first does not decompose.
cards.recall: Before revealing: the naive framing loops over which balloon to burst FIRST, and it does not work. Say why, and say what changes when you loop over which balloon bursts LAST.
useWhen: Burst balloons
Matrix chain multiplication
Minimum cost to merge stones or cut a stick
Remove boxes and similar interference problems
Any interval DP where neighbours change as you act
template: # dp[i][j] = max coins from bursting everything strictly inside (i, j)
# Loop over k = the LAST balloon burst in that open interval.
# When k is last, i and j are still standing, so left and right are independent.
for length in range(2, n):          # window width in the padded array
for k in range(i + 1, j):   # k bursts LAST
keyInsights: First-move framing fails because bursting changes who the neighbours are, so the two sides are not independent subproblems
Last-move framing keeps i and j alive throughout, which is exactly what restores independence
The padding with 1s removes every boundary special case, the same trick as the zero row in two-string DP
cards.trap: 'Why n^3?' n^2 intervals times n choices of last move. If you say n^2 you have not understood your own loops.

cards.title: Clone with a Map
patterns: Old node to new node map
cards.trigger: Deep copy a structure that may contain cycles or shared references.
cards.recall: Write clone graph from memory. Then answer the ordering question: why must you put the new node into the map BEFORE recursing into its neighbours?
useWhen: Clone an undirected graph
Copy a linked list with random pointers
Deep copy any object graph with cycles
Serialize and rebuild a DAG
Any structural copy where identity must be preserved
template: if n in made: return made[n]     # already cloned, cycle-safe
# Random-pointer linked list, two passes, no recursion:
#   pass 1: create every copy and map old -> new
keyInsights: Registering before recursing is what stops a cycle from recursing forever. It is the whole correctness argument
The map does double duty: visited set and old-to-new translation table
The two-pass version for the random-pointer list avoids recursion entirely and is easier to defend on deep inputs
cards.trap: 'Do it with O(1) extra space for the random-pointer list.' Interleave copies into the original list, wire the random pointers, then unweave. Know that trick exists.
